name: Pyro Probabilistic Programming for Lottery — Variational LSTM with Uncertainty Quantification
key_paper: Bingham et al., 'Pyro: Deep Universal Probabilistic Programming', JMLR 2019 (v.20, no.28); Chen et al., 'Stochastic Video Generation with a Learned Prior' (ICML 2019) for probabilistic LSTM pattern; Fortunato et al., 'Bayesian Recurrent Neural Networks', arXiv 2017 for Bayesian LSTM background
algorithm_description: Pyro is a deep probabilistic programming language (PPL) built on PyTorch that enables specifying probabilistic models as Python programs with stochastic primitives (pyro.sample). Inference is performed via Stochastic Variational Inference (SVI): a guide (variational distribution q_phi) approximates the true posterior p(z|x) by minimizing the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) via gradient descent. For a probabilistic LSTM head, the model defines latent variables z_t at each timestep (or at the output layer) drawn from a prior (e.g., Normal(0,1)); the guide learns approximate posterior parameters (mu_phi, sigma_phi) conditioned on the observed sequence. The decoder maps latent samples through the output head to produce distributions over lottery numbers rather than point estimates. At prediction time, Monte Carlo sampling over the posterior yields calibrated uncertainty intervals: running the model N times with different z samples produces N plausible play candidates whose spread reflects the model's epistemic uncertainty about which numbers are likely.
action_space_handling: Pyro does not impose a specific action space structure — the action space is defined by the model program. For lottery number prediction, the output is a multi-hot vector of length N (50 for LottoMax). In the variational LSTM formulation, the model outputs a Bernoulli distribution parameter vector p in [0,1]^N for each number (or a Categorical for selecting exactly k), with uncertainty quantified via the posterior over latent variables z. The action space is flat/factored: each number is sampled independently from its marginal posterior distribution, which misses inter-number correlations but is straightforward to implement. An autoregressive extension (each number conditioned on previous) is possible but requires custom guide design and is not native to standard Pyro tutorials.
how_combinatorial_output_is_formed: In the standard Pyro probabilistic LSTM setup, the model outputs a vector of Bernoulli logits (one per number in the pool). To form a play of exactly k distinct numbers, two approaches exist: (1) Threshold/top-k post-processing: sample the posterior predictive distribution N times (each sample is a full probability vector p in [0,1]^N), then take the top-k indices by probability — this enforces cardinality but loses calibration; (2) Gumbel-top-k: treat the Bernoulli logits as unnormalized scores and apply differentiable top-k sampling (Kool et al. 2019) after posterior sampling, preserving approximate differentiability. The most common practical approach in lottery-nn context would be posterior sampling (100-1000 samples) followed by top-k selection and frequency aggregation across samples to generate a ranked list of candidate numbers.
sequential_generation_strategy: Jointly (flat multi-hot) by default in the standard Pyro probabilistic LSTM. The LSTM processes the historical draw sequence and produces a context vector; the variational head maps this to per-number Bernoulli parameters. Each number's probability is computed independently of others in the same draw — no autoregressive conditioning within a single play. Inter-draw temporal correlations ARE modeled (the LSTM sequence models how number frequencies evolve over time), but intra-play correlations (e.g., that number 7 and 14 tend to co-occur) are not captured. A fully autoregressive within-play model (like a pointer network) would require a different architecture and is not the standard Pyro LSTM pattern.
gradient_estimator_type: Pyro's SVI uses the reparameterization trick (pathwise gradient estimator) for continuous latent variables (Normal, Beta, etc.) — this is low-variance and stable. For discrete latent variables (Bernoulli, Categorical), Pyro supports several estimators: (1) REINFORCE (score function estimator) — high variance, requires baseline; (2) Relaxed/Gumbel-softmax via pyro.distributions.RelaxedBernoulli or RelaxedOneHotCategorical — enables reparameterization for discrete variables with a temperature hyperparameter; (3) TraceEnum_ELBO — exact enumeration for small discrete spaces, not scalable to N=50. For a probabilistic LSTM with continuous latent z (most common design), the reparameterization trick applies cleanly and provides low-variance gradients, making SVI training stable even on small datasets.
combinatorial_constraint_enforcement: Pyro does not natively enforce the 'exactly k distinct numbers' constraint within a probabilistic model. Enforcement options: (1) Post-hoc top-k on the mean posterior predictive — simplest, breaks differentiability; (2) Constrained distributions: define a custom PyTorch distribution for k-subset sampling (e.g., using the PlackettLuce distribution, available in pyro.distributions) which assigns probability to permutations and naturally yields sets of size k via top-k; (3) Soft constraint via loss: add a penalty term to the ELBO that penalizes expected cardinality deviating from k — integrates cleanly with SVI; (4) Acceptance-rejection in posterior predictive sampling: draw samples, reject those with wrong cardinality, reweight — valid but slow. The PlackettLuce approach is the most principled Pyro-native method for set-valued outputs.
sample_efficiency_rating: medium — Pyro's variational inference with informative priors (e.g., Beta priors encoding historical base rates) is more data-efficient than maximum-likelihood point estimates because the prior regularizes parameter estimates when data is scarce. On fewer than 200 draws, the prior dominates the posterior, which is both a strength (prevents overfitting) and a limitation (predictions are heavily influenced by prior assumptions). Bayesian LSTM models have been shown to provide reasonable uncertainty estimates with as few as 50-200 training examples in regression tasks (Fortunato et al. 2017). However, the ELBO optimization itself can be unstable on very small datasets due to high-variance mini-batch gradient estimates of the KL term. Using the full dataset per SVI step (batch size = all draws) mitigates this at the cost of scalability — acceptable for ~100-200 lottery draws.
regularization_built_in: Multiple inherent regularization mechanisms: (1) KL divergence penalty in ELBO: KL(q_phi(z) || p(z)) penalizes the posterior from deviating too far from the prior, acting as a Bayesian weight decay; (2) Prior specification: informative priors on output logits (e.g., Beta(alpha, beta) encoding historical frequency) regularize predictions toward base rates; (3) Dropout MC (via pyro.contrib.bnn or manual nn.Dropout with training=True at test time) provides an ensemble effect; (4) Automatic regularization via model structure: latent variable z forces information bottleneck through a low-dimensional space; (5) Weight uncertainty: BNN extension (Bayes by Backprop, available in Pyro) places distributions over network weights, preventing overconfident parameter estimates on small data.
known_failure_modes_on_small_data: 1) Posterior collapse: the KL term dominates the ELBO on small datasets, causing the guide to collapse to the prior (q_phi approx p) — the latent variables z carry no information and predictions revert to base rates. Mitigation: KL annealing (beta-VAE schedule, gradually increasing KL weight from 0 to 1 during training). 2) Guide expressiveness mismatch: mean-field guides (diagonal Normal) may poorly approximate true posteriors for recurrent models with strong temporal correlations — normalizing flow guides (Pyro supports IAF, RealNVP) improve this but increase complexity. 3) ELBO instability: with fewer than 50 training points and 1-sample Monte Carlo ELBO estimates, gradient variance is very high. Fix: use multiple ELBO samples per step (num_particles in Pyro SVI). 4) Prior sensitivity: results can be highly sensitive to prior hyperparameter choices when data is sparse — requires prior sensitivity analysis which adds experimental overhead.
data_regime_evidence: Pyro and variational Bayesian RNNs have been tested across a range of data regimes, but specific benchmarks on fewer than 200 sequential discrete examples are limited. Fortunato et al. (2017, 'Bayesian Recurrent Neural Networks') show Bayes-by-Backprop LSTM improves over standard LSTM on Penn Treebank language modeling with reduced data splits, but minimum sample sizes tested are ~1000. Pyro's own tutorials demonstrate SVI on small Gaussian mixture models and coin-flipping examples (n < 50) where inference is exact, but time-series tasks with recurrent models are not benchmarked below n=500. Blundell et al. (2015, 'Weight Uncertainty in Neural Networks', ICML) show BNNs outperform MAP on MNIST with reduced training sets (down to 1000 examples), but this is image classification, not sequential combinatorial prediction. [uncertain: minimum_training_samples_tested for probabilistic LSTM below 200] [uncertain: whether uncertainty intervals remain calibrated on n < 100 sequential draws]
convergence_guarantees_small_n: [uncertain] SVI with reparameterization gradients converges to a local optimum of the ELBO under standard stochastic optimization conditions (Robbins-Monro conditions on learning rate schedule), but finite-sample bounds on ELBO approximation quality are not established for small n. The ELBO is a lower bound on log p(x), so maximizing it is a valid objective regardless of sample size, but the tightness of the bound (gap between ELBO and log p(x)) depends on guide expressiveness and is not quantified in small-data regimes. Kingma & Welling (2013) provide asymptotic guarantees. For n < 200, the main practical risk is not divergence but poor ELBO optima due to multiple local minima in guide parameter space — empirically mitigated by warm restarts and learning rate scheduling.
reward_distribution_handling: Pyro handles skewed reward distributions naturally through the probabilistic model's likelihood specification. For lottery's ~95% zero-hit regime: the model's output distribution (Bernoulli per number) can be calibrated to reflect true low-probability events via the posterior. Importantly, Pyro enables explicit uncertainty quantification — when training data shows that most number combinations lose, the posterior predictive distribution will assign low probability mass to most combinations, and the uncertainty intervals will be wide (high epistemic uncertainty), which is the correct and honest behavior. Unlike point-estimate models that may overconfidently predict specific numbers, the Bayesian approach acknowledges that the lottery is nearly unpredictable. Minimum draws for stable SVI learning: approximately 50-100 draws, though meaningful posterior updating requires at least 30-50 non-trivial observations.
credit_assignment_granularity: Number-level credit assignment is native to the Pyro probabilistic LSTM approach. Since the model outputs per-number Bernoulli probabilities (one per number in the pool), training with binary labels per number (did number i appear in this draw?) directly updates each number's posterior probability independently. This is exactly the semi-bandit feedback structure: observing a draw (3, 7, 18, 24, 31, 42, bonus=15) provides a binary signal for all 49/50 numbers simultaneously, not just the play-level win/loss. The ELBO update uses all N binary observations per draw, giving N times more gradient signal per draw than play-level-only methods. This is a significant advantage over methods that only receive play-level reward.
diversity_mechanism: Diversity emerges naturally from posterior predictive sampling: drawing multiple plays from the posterior predictive distribution (by first sampling z from q_phi(z|x), then sampling numbers from p(numbers|z)) produces plays that differ according to the posterior uncertainty. When uncertainty is high (as expected for lottery), the spread of sampled plays is wide. Additional diversity mechanisms: (1) Temperature scaling on the Bernoulli logits at prediction time (already present in lottery-nn via config.TEMPERATURE); (2) Explicit diversity through repulsive particle variational inference (Liu & Wang 2016, Stein Variational Gradient Descent — available in Pyro) which pushes posterior particles apart; (3) Mixture guide: using a mixture of Gaussians as the variational posterior (pyro.infer.autoguide.AutoMixtureLowRankMultivariateNormal) increases diversity of sampled plays naturally.
offline_vs_online_rl_compatibility: Fully compatible with offline training from a fixed historical dataset — this is Pyro's primary use case. SVI trains the variational parameters on the observed draw history without any online environment interaction. No live draws are needed during training. The historical CSV (draws.csv, draws_649.csv, draws_dailygrand.csv) is the complete training set, processed once per epoch. After each new real draw is logged via main.py log, the model can be updated by running one additional SVI pass over the full dataset (or fine-tuned with a few steps on the new observation). This is ideal for the lottery-nn workflow of weekly updates. Pyro also supports online Bayesian updating in principle (sequential SVI or Kalman filter-style updates), though this requires additional implementation beyond the standard SVI loop.
key_dependencies: pyro-ppl (pip install pyro-ppl) — core dependency, installs pyro and pyro.distributions on top of PyTorch. No other mandatory dependencies beyond what lottery-nn already uses (torch, numpy, pandas). Optional: funsor (for exact inference with enumeration, pip install funsor), numpyro (JAX-based alternative, not needed if staying PyTorch). Pyro version >= 1.8 recommended for full SVI and autoguide support. As of 2025 Pyro-PPL is actively maintained by Uber AI / community.
estimated_lines_of_code: 300-450 lines — probabilistic LSTM model definition in Pyro syntax (~80 lines: prior specs, pyro.sample calls for z, likelihood), mean-field guide definition or AutoDiagonalNormal autoguide (~30 lines), SVI training loop with ELBO logging (~60 lines), posterior predictive sampling function with top-k play generation (~60 lines), integration with SharedLotteryTransformer encoder as deterministic prefix + stochastic head (~80 lines), prediction uncertainty reporting + integration into main_swarm.py predict command (~60 lines), config additions for num_particles/KL_beta/prior_scale (~20 lines). Total ~390 lines excluding boilerplate.
transfer_learning_compatibility: High compatibility via a clean encoder-head split. The existing SharedLotteryTransformer encoder (pretrained, ~253K params) can be used as a deterministic feature extractor: its output context vector h_t is passed to the new Pyro probabilistic head as a conditioning variable. Only the probabilistic head (latent variable z, guide parameters, output Bernoulli logits) is stochastic and trained via SVI — the encoder can be either frozen (fastest, ~0 additional encoder compute) or fine-tuned jointly (more powerful but risks ELBO instability on small data). Recommended approach: freeze the encoder for the first 50 SVI epochs, then unfreeze with a small learning rate (1e-5) for the encoder vs. 1e-3 for the guide. This is analogous to how VAEs are often trained with a pretrained encoder backbone.
specific_application_in_project: In lottery-nn, Pyro would add a probabilistic output head on top of the existing SharedLotteryTransformer backbone. Specifically: (1) Replace the deterministic linear output layer in model_swarm.py with a Pyro model/guide pair — the guide learns per-number posterior distributions (mu_i, sigma_i) over Bernoulli logits for each number in the pool; (2) Training via SVI on historical draws.csv/draws_649.csv/draws_dailygrand.csv using binary supervision (did number i appear in draw t? yes/no for all i); (3) At prediction time, run 200-500 posterior predictive samples, aggregate into a probability vector with uncertainty bands, and select the top-k numbers as the recommended play along with confidence intervals; (4) The uncertainty output becomes a new field in the predict command: 'high confidence' numbers (low variance across samples) vs 'uncertain' numbers (high variance), giving the user actionable information; (5) The swarm_state.json can store per-lottery posterior parameters as a lightweight serializable representation of the Bayesian model state. Applies to all three lotteries using per-lottery output heads, consistent with the existing swarm architecture. Recommended for Phase 3 after Actor-Critic (Phase 2) is complete.
replaces_or_extends: Extends — adds a stochastic Pyro probabilistic head on top of the existing SharedLotteryTransformer encoder without replacing it. The deterministic LSTM/Transformer backbone remains; the output layer becomes a variational inference module. Prediction output is extended from a single point-estimate play to a play with per-number uncertainty scores.
existing_open_source_implementations: 1) Official Pyro tutorials (pyro.ai/examples): 'Bayesian Regression', 'Deep Markov Model' (probabilistic LSTM analog), 'Time Series Forecasting' — all directly relevant patterns; 2) pyro-ppl/pyro GitHub: github.com/pyro-ppl/pyro — actively maintained, 8000+ stars as of 2025, includes autoguide modules for minimal boilerplate; 3) Deep Markov Model (Krishnan et al. 2017): reference probabilistic RNN implementation in Pyro, directly applicable to sequential draw prediction; 4) pyro-ppl/numpyro: JAX version, faster on GPU but less relevant here since lottery-nn uses PyTorch; 5) Blundell et al. BNN reference in Pyro: pyro.contrib.bnn provides BayesianLinear layers for weight-space uncertainty (alternative to latent variable z approach); 6) Pyro autoguides (pyro.infer.autoguide): AutoDiagonalNormal, AutoLowRankMultivariateNormal — drastically reduce guide boilerplate to 2-3 lines of code.
benchmark_results: Pyro (Bingham et al. JMLR 2019): demonstrated scalable SVI on large-scale Bayesian neural networks and VAEs; key result: SVI scales to millions of parameters with reparameterization gradients. Deep Markov Model (Krishnan et al. 2017, AAAI 2017): probabilistic LSTM achieved better calibration than deterministic LSTM on sequential clinical data (MIMIC-III, ~10K patients) — not small data, but validates the architecture pattern. Fortunato et al. (2017, Bayes by Backprop LSTM): 10-20% perplexity improvement over standard LSTM on Penn Treebank language modeling, with meaningful uncertainty estimates; tested down to ~1/10 of training data (~100K tokens, not draws). Dropout as Bayesian Approximation (Gal & Ghahramani 2016, ICML): MC Dropout (implementable in Pyro or vanilla PyTorch) showed well-calibrated uncertainty on MNIST and regression tasks with limited data — this simpler Pyro-compatible approach may be more practical for lottery-nn at n < 200. No benchmarks specific to lottery or combinatorial number selection tasks.
notable_use_cases: 1) Clinical time series prediction (Deep Markov Model, Krishnan 2017): probabilistic LSTM for patient state evolution — sequential discrete observations with sparse informative events, directly analogous to lottery draw sequences; 2) Financial time series uncertainty quantification: multiple papers use Pyro's SVI for stock return distribution modeling, leveraging the fat-tail properties of posterior predictive distributions — structurally similar to lottery's highly skewed reward; 3) Demand forecasting with uncertainty (Amazon DeepAR, Salinas et al. 2020): probabilistic RNN for sparse intermittent demand — closest published analog to sparse lottery hits, though DeepAR uses a separate implementation; 4) Drug activity prediction (Ramsundar et al., DeepChem): Bayesian neural networks via Pyro for molecular property prediction from limited assay data (<200 labeled molecules per target) — validates small-data probabilistic NN viability; 5) Anomaly detection in sequential data: Pyro-based VAE-LSTM models identify anomalous patterns, relevant since rare lottery hits can be viewed as anomaly detection in reverse.
